title: Sliding Window Maximum with a Monotonic Deque
prompt: A real-time SLA monitor ingests 500,000 latency samples/sec per shard and must emit the exact rolling maximum latency over the last `k = 10,000` samples (and in a variant, over a `W = 5,000 ms` time window). The current implementation uses a max-heap (`PriorityQueue` / `heapq`) with lazy deletion, which grows beyond `100k` stale nodes during bursts and triggers `p99` spikes and GC pauses. Design a strict `O(1)` amortized-per-event sliding window maximum engine.

spark.summary: Naive O(N*k) scans or O(N log k) max-heaps with lazy deletion cause GC pressure and p99 latency spikes on 500k events/sec streams; a monotonic decreasing deque computes exact sliding-window maxima in strict O(N) time and O(k) space.
spark.keyTakeaway: Store indices in a monotonic decreasing deque, evicting expired front indices and smaller back indices so every element is pushed and popped at most once.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** A real-time SLA monitor ingesting `500,000` latency samples/sec (`2 microseconds` average budget per event) must emit the exact rolling maximum over the last `k = 10,000` samples (or `W = 5,000 ms`).

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Lazy-Deletion Max-Heap Bloat vs. Bounded O(1) Deque (500k/s Stream -> Max-Heap (Lazy) -> Monotonic Deque); Three-Step Per-Event State Transition (1. EVICT FRONT -> 2. PRUNE BACK -> 3. PUSH & EMIT).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Two subtle mistakes ruin an otherwise good deque solution: **Using Python `list.pop(0)`**: Shifts all remaining elements in `O(k)`, degrading total runtime back to `O(N * k)`. Maintain a deque of indices whose corresponding values are strictly decreasing from front to back: **Front Expiration (`O(1)`)**: If `dq[0] <= i - k` (or `ts - dq[0].ts > W` for time-based windows), `popleft()`.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Monotonic deques are used wherever rolling extrema must be tracked over high-frequency streams: **Real-Time APM & SLA Monitors**: Computes rolling p100/max latency over `W = 5,000 ms` windows with zero heap churn.

learningJourney.title: Lazy-deletion heap bloat and p99 GC pauses under burst traffic
learningJourney.explanation:
Using a max-heap (`PriorityQueue` / `heapq`) with lazy deletion fails under high-rate streams:

1. **100k+ Stale Heap Nodes**: When monotonic bursts keep a large old value at the root or delay eviction, the heap swells far beyond `k`.
2. **GC & `O(log N)` Allocation Churn**: Allocating `(value, index)` tuples at `500k/sec` triggers frequent GC pauses that breach the `2 us` budget.

learningJourney.title: Common implementation bugs: list.pop(0) and storing raw values
learningJourney.explanation:
Two subtle mistakes ruin an otherwise good deque solution:

- **Using Python `list.pop(0)`**: Shifts all remaining elements in `O(k)`, degrading total runtime back to `O(N * k)`. Always use `collections.deque.popleft()` (or a fixed ring buffer).
- **Storing raw values instead of indices / `(ts, val)`**: Without the index or timestamp, you cannot tell in `O(1)` whether `dq[0]` has expired from the window.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise solution: Monotonic Decreasing Deque of Indices / Timestamps
learningJourney.explanation:
Maintain a deque of indices whose corresponding values are strictly decreasing from front to back:

- **Front Expiration (`O(1)`)**: If `dq[0] <= i - k` (or `ts - dq[0].ts > W` for time-based windows), `popleft()`.
- **Back Dominance Pruning**: While `nums[dq[-1]] <= val`, `pop()` from the back—any older element smaller than or equal to `val` can *never* be the maximum of any future window.
- **Strict `O(N)` Time, `O(k)` Space**: Every element is pushed once and popped at most once (`<= 2N` operations total), keeping memory strictly `<= k`.

sectionDiagram.title: Three-Step Per-Event State Transition
sectionDiagram.summary: Each element enters and leaves the deque at most once, guaranteeing strict O(N) total time and O(k) space.

learningJourney.title: Where monotonic deques power streaming & rate-limiting systems
learningJourney.explanation:
Monotonic deques are used wherever rolling extrema must be tracked over high-frequency streams:

- **Real-Time APM & SLA Monitors**: Computes rolling p100/max latency over `W = 5,000 ms` windows with zero heap churn.
- **Adaptive Concurrency & Congestion Control**: Tracks `min_rtt` over a sliding time window (e.g., BBR / Envoy).
- **Financial Tick & Order-Book Engines**: Maintains rolling high/low price bounds in `O(1)` amortized time.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is the monotonic decreasing deque guaranteed to run in `O(N)` total time even though it has an inner `while` loop?

options.text: Each of the N elements is pushed onto the deque once and popped at most once, bounding total deque operations to 2N
options.feedback: Correct: amortized across the stream, every element performs at most one push and one pop.

options.text: The inner while loop only runs on the first k elements
options.feedback: The while loop can run on any element, but total pops across the whole array cannot exceed N.

options.text: Python's deque uses a red-black tree internally
options.feedback: collections.deque is a doubly-linked block list with O(1) append/pop at both ends.
